title: Modules and Packages
summary: A module is a Python file you can reuse. A package groups related modules together.
introduction: A module is a Python file you can reuse. A package groups related modules together. Think of borrowing a useful page from a recipe book. Use import to bring in a tool, then learn how to keep extra tools organised.
learningObjectives: Import modules and individual names with import, from and as
Create your own module and import it from another file
Explain what the __name__ check does and when to use it
Organise modules into a package and find useful standard-library modules

blocks.title: imports.py
blocks.code:
import math
from datetime import date
from statistics import mean, median
import random as rnd

print(math.sqrt(2))
print(date(2026, 11, 15).strftime("%A %d %B %Y"))
print(mean([2, 4, 9]), median([2, 4, 9]))
rnd.seed(7)
print(rnd.randint(1, 100))
print(date(2026, 12, 25) - date(2026, 11, 15))

blocks.text: `import math` loads the module once and gives you a namespace: every name inside it is reached as `math.something`. `from ... import ...` copies specific names into your file so you call them bare. `as` renames, either to shorten (`import numpy as np` is universal) or to avoid a clash with one of your own names. Avoid `from module import *`: it dumps unknown names into your file and makes it impossible to see where a function came from.
Any `.py` file is a module. Put reusable functions in `shapes.py`, then import it from a script in the same folder; the module's name is the file name without the extension.

blocks.title: shapes.py
blocks.code:
"""Area helpers for simple shapes."""

import math

def circle_area(radius):
    return math.pi * radius ** 2

def rectangle_area(width, height):
    return width * height

print("shapes module loaded")

blocks.title: main.py
blocks.code:
import shapes
from shapes import rectangle_area

print(shapes.circle_area(2))
print(rectangle_area(3, 4))
print(shapes.__doc__)

blocks.title: python main.py
blocks.content:
shapes module loaded
12.566370614359172
12
Area helpers for simple shapes.

blocks.text: Notice `shapes module loaded` at the top of the second output: importing runs the whole module file once, top to bottom, including that stray `print`. Function definitions are statements too, and running them is what creates the functions. A module is cached after its first import, so a second `import shapes` elsewhere in the program does not run it again. The docstring at the top of the file becomes the module's `__doc__`.

Every module has a `__name__` variable. When a file is run directly, Python sets it to `"__main__"`; when the file is imported, it holds the module's name, here `"shapes"`. Testing it separates what a file does when executed from what it provides when imported, which lets a module double as a script without side effects for importers:

blocks.title: shapes.py

blocks.text: Run `python main.py` again and the test line no longer appears: inside an import, `__name__` is `"shapes"`, so the block is skipped. Put a script's top-level code in a `main()` function and call it from this block; it keeps the module importable from tests.

A **package** is a folder of modules. Create a folder `geometry/` with an `__init__.py` file (it may be empty or hold a docstring; since Python 3.3 the file is optional, but keeping it is the convention) plus one module per topic, and the modules become importable as `geometry.units`, `geometry.shapes` and so on. Folders inside folders make sub-packages, which is how large libraries such as `django.db.models` are organised.

blocks.title: geometry/units.py
app.py
blocks.code:
import geometry
from geometry import units
from geometry.units import inches_to_cm

print(geometry.__doc__)
print(units.cm_to_inches(100))
print(inches_to_cm(10))

blocks.text: Dotted names follow the folder structure. `from geometry import units` gives you the module, `from geometry.units import inches_to_cm` a single function; both are common, and which one you pick is about readability at the call site.

blocks.title: Do not name your file after a module
blocks.text: A file called `random.py` or `json.py` in your project folder shadows the real module: `import random` loads *your* file, and `random.randint` fails with `AttributeError: module 'random' has no attribute 'randint'`. Python 3.13 adds a hint to that message (`consider renaming ... since it has the same name as the standard library module`). Pick specific names such as `dice.py`; the same applies to folders.

Fetch URLs, serve a folder over HTTP locally

blocks.text: Python 3.13 removed 19 old modules that nobody maintained (`cgi`, `telnetlib`, `crypt` and others), so a very old tutorial may import something that no longer exists; the replacement is usually a third-party package. Those come from PyPI via `pip`, covered in [Virtual Environments and pip](/tutorials/python/virtual-environments). Whatever you need, check the standard library first: a solution that needs no installation is easier to share.

questions.question: You run `python tools.py` directly. What is the value of `__name__` inside tools.py?
questions.explanation: The file being executed is always `"__main__"`. It would be `"tools"` only if another file imported it.

questions.question: `from math import *` is the recommended way to import because it saves typing.
questions.explanation: Star imports hide where names come from and can silently overwrite your own variables. Import the module, or the specific names you use.

seo.title: Python Modules and Packages – import and __main__
